mainTopic: Reading witnesses' signatures on two side-by-side גיטין, and the משנה on where and how witnesses sign a גט
overview: The amud opens in the middle of a discussion of two גיטין written side by side, with four witnesses signing beneath them. The גמרא first shows that a father's name spilling under the second גט is part of one signature, because people neither sign with their father's name nor turn it into a signing symbol. It then asks why each pair of witnesses cannot validate its own גט. זעירי's teaching says both are valid. Our משנה disagrees because of גונדלית, the worry that the witnesses signed in reverse and really belong to a different גט. A new משנה follows. It rules that a גט may continue into a second column if the witnesses sign below. It explains which גט is valid when two are written on one sheet with signatures between them, and it allows mixed languages, a scribe plus one witness, short signatures, and nicknames. The גמרא then worries that a two-column גט might be pieced together from two cut-up גיטין. רבי אבא in the name of רב answers that there is blank space below the first column, and the discussion of this answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Maybe the witness signed the second גט with his father's name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the name יעקב under the second גט could be a real signature by ראובן, using his father's name.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe he signed using his father's name!
steps.whatsHappening: The witness's signature runs across both גיטין, with his father's name (יעקב) landing under the second one. The גמרא asks: maybe ראובן really signed the second גט, just by writing his father's name?
steps.deeperAnalysis: If יעקב counts as a separate signature, then ראובן signed both גיטין, and our reading of the signatures falls apart. The challenge tries to turn one long signature into two short ones.

keyTerms.meaning: But maybe, the opening of a challenge

phrases.english: But maybe he signed with his father's name!
phrases.notes: He means: maybe the word יעקב under the second get is ראובן's own signature on that get.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the earlier reading, outside this text, that the spilled-over father's name belongs to one signature.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assumption that 'ראובן בן יעקב' is a single signature on the first get
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The father's name standing alone under the second get could be a signature in its own right.

steps.title: People do not sign with their father's name instead of their own
steps.stepSummary: A person does not drop his own name to sign with his father's name.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person does not leave out his own name and sign his father's name.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge: normal people sign their own name, not their father's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since nobody signs with only his father's name, the word יעקב must be the end of the signature 'ראובן בן יעקב'. It is not a separate signature on the second get.

phrases.english: A person does not leave out his own name
and sign his father's name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The father's name could be a separate signature.
steps.terutzMaskana: People sign their own name, so יעקב is part of ראובן's single signature.

steps.title: Maybe he used his father's name as a signature symbol
steps.stepSummary: Some רבנן signed with a symbol instead of their name. Maybe ראובן used his father's name as his symbol.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe he made his father's name his signature symbol. After all, רב drew a fish, רבי חנינא a palm, רב חסדא a ס, רב הושעיא an ע, and רבה בר רב הונא drew a sail!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes again. A signature does not have to be your name; some great רבנן signed with a picture or a letter. So maybe יעקב was ראובן's personal symbol.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 said people sign their own name. This challenge answers that a signature can be any mark a person regularly uses. So the father's name could be ראובן's mark, which would make it a real signature under the second גט.

keyTerms.meaning: A sign or symbol used as a signature
A palm branch or date palm

steps.confusionAlert: These רבנן were not breaking a rule. A regular personal mark counts as a real signature. That is exactly why the challenge is strong.

phrases.english: But maybe he made it a symbol,
phrases.notes: 'It' means his father's name: maybe he used יעקב as his regular signing mark.

phrases.english: for רב would draw a fish,
רבי חנינא, a palm,
רב חסדא, a samekh,
רב הושעיא, an ayin,

phrases.aramaic: רַבָּה בַּר רַב הוּנָא צָיֵיר מָכוּתָא!
phrases.english: and רבה בר רב הונא would draw a sail!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that people only sign with their own name
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Known רבנן signed with symbols, so a non-name mark like the father's name could still be a valid signature.

steps.title: No one would dare use his father's name as a symbol
steps.stepSummary: It would be disrespectful to turn one's father's name into a signing mark, so no one would do it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person would not be so brazen as to make his father's name a symbol.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that using your father's name as a casual signing mark would be חוצפה, and a person would not do that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Symbols are fine in general, but not this one, out of respect for a parent. So יעקב must still be part of ראובן's single signature on the first גט. The earlier reading stands.
steps.whatToRemember: The father's name under the second גט is not a separate signature. People do not sign with their father's name, and they would not disrespect it by making it a symbol.

phrases.english: A person is not so brazen
as to make his father's name a symbol.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא חֲצִיף אִינִישׁ לְשַׁוּוֹיֵי לִשְׁמָא דַאֲבוּהּ סִימָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 3 and closes this line of questioning.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the case: symbols are allowed, but not the father's name
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The father's name could serve as a personal signing symbol.
steps.terutzMaskana: Respect for a father rules this out, so the name is part of one signature.

steps.title: Why not validate each גט by its own pair of witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why one גט is not validated by the Hebrew witnesses and the other by the Greek witnesses. A גט can be written in one language and signed in another.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let this גט be valid through the two Hebrew witnesses, and that גט through the two Greek witnesses. For we learned: a גט written in Hebrew with its witnesses signed in Greek, or written in Greek with its witnesses signed in Hebrew, is כשר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new challenge to the משנה. There are two pairs of witnesses, so let each pair validate a different גט. A מתניתין also teaches that the language of the signatures does not have to match the גט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה made only one גט valid. But we have four witnesses, enough for two גיטין. The quoted משנה removes the possible objection that Greek witnesses cannot sign a Hebrew גט, or the reverse. Steps 6 to 8 work out the answer.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the next discussion about how the witnesses' signatures are arranged and why they cannot simply be split between the two גיטין.

phrases.english: But let this one be validated by the two Hebrew witnesses,
and let that one be validated by the two Greek witnesses,
as we learned: a get that one wrote in Hebrew
phrases.notes: This is quoted from the next משנה in the פרק.

phrases.english: and its witnesses in Greek, or in Greek and its witnesses in Hebrew,
is valid!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the signature-reading question and challenges the משנה's ruling that only one get is valid.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that only the get read with the first witnesses is כשר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Each get has two available witnesses, and mixed languages are allowed, so both גיטין should be valid.

steps.title: Blocking the answer of the two-line gap
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא heads off a possible answer. Someone might say the Greek witnesses are too far below the second גט to count. But חזקיה rules that a gap filled in, even with relatives' signatures, is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you will say: since the second pair of signatures is two lines away from the גט, it does not work. But didn't חזקיה say that if the gap was filled, even with relatives, the document is valid?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is still pushing its question from Step 5. It shuts down one possible way to answer it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, if the witnesses' signatures are two lines below the text, the document is invalid, because something could be slipped into the gap. Here the gap under the second get is filled by the Hebrew witnesses' signatures. חזקיה says that a filled gap is fine, even if it is filled with signatures that do not count, like those of relatives. So the gap is no reason to throw out the second get.

keyTerms.meaning: Relatives, who cannot serve as witnesses
An early אמורא whose rule is quoted here

phrases.english: And if you will say,
since it is two lines away, it is not valid;
phrases.notes: He means the Greek witnesses' signatures, which sit two lines below the second get because the Hebrew signatures are in between.

phrases.english: but didn't חזקיה say:
if he filled it with relatives, it is valid!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא, כֵּיוָן דְּמוּפְלָג בִּשְׁנֵי שִׁיטִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the קשיא of Step 5 by ruling out a possible answer in advance
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that only the get read with the first witnesses is valid
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The gap is filled by the Hebrew signatures, and חזקיה says a filled gap does not invalidate. So the Greek witnesses should validate the second get.

steps.title: זעירי holds that both גיטין are valid
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that זעירי's version of the teaching does say both גיטין are valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: Indeed, זעירי teaches: both of them are valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by bringing a teaching that זעירי passes down, which agrees with it: both גיטין are valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question was a good one, and זעירי's teaching follows exactly that logic: the second get is validated by the Greek witnesses. This leaves the question of why our משנה disagrees, which the גמרא answers next.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who passes down a different teaching on this case
He teaches (a ברייתא or teaching passed down)

phrases.english: Indeed, זעירי teaches:
both of them are valid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא by showing that a תנא does hold this way
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a תנא who agrees with the question's logic
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everyone must hold that only the first get is valid
steps.terutzMaskana: זעירי holds that both גיטין are valid; only our תנא disagrees

steps.title: Our תנא worries that the witnesses signed in reverse
steps.stepSummary: Our תנא disagrees because the Greek witnesses may have signed in a reversed way, so all four may really have signed the first גט.
steps.simpleTranslation: And our תנא? Perhaps they signed in reverse, and all of them signed on one גט.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the תנא of our משנה does not agree with זעירי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worry is called גונדלית: the bottom witnesses may have signed in a reversed way. Then signatures that look like they sit under the second גט may really belong to the first. If all four witnesses signed only the first גט, the second גט has no witnesses at all.
steps.confusionAlert: Our תנא is not saying the witnesses certainly signed in reverse. It is only a possibility, but that doubt is enough to keep us from relying on the second get.

phrases.english: And our תנא, why does he disagree?
perhaps they signed in reverse,
and all of them signed on one get.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning of the משנה, which disagrees with זעירי
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a factual doubt about how the witnesses signed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Greek signatures plainly belong to the second get
steps.terutzMaskana: They may have been signed in reverse and belong to the first get, so the second get cannot be relied on

steps.title: The mixed case: why not pair up the witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא turns to the משנה's second case. It asks why the first Hebrew and Greek pair cannot validate one get and the second pair the other, since a get signed by one Hebrew and one Greek witness is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: one Hebrew witness and one Greek witness. Let this גט be validated by one Hebrew and one Greek witness, and that גט by one Hebrew and one Greek witness. For we learned: one Hebrew witness and one Greek witness is valid!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next case in the משנה, where the signatures go Hebrew, Greek, Hebrew, Greek and both גיטין are invalid. Then it challenges that ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה rules both גיטין invalid in this case. But another משנה teaches that a גט with one Hebrew and one Greek witness is valid. So why not split the four witnesses into two mixed pairs, one pair for each גט?

phrases.aramaic: עֵד אֶחָד עִבְרִי וְעֵד אֶחָד יְוָנִי.
phrases.english: The משנה says: one Hebrew witness and one Greek witness.
phrases.notes: This is a quote of the next case in the משנה, where both גיטין are ruled invalid.

phrases.english: But let this get be validated

phrases.aramaic: בְּעֵד אֶחָד עִבְרִי וְעֵד אֶחָד יְוָנִי,
phrases.english: by one Hebrew witness and one Greek witness,

phrases.aramaic: וְהַאי בְּעֵד אֶחָד עִבְרִי וְעֵד אֶחָד יְוָנִי –
phrases.english: and that get by one Hebrew witness and one Greek witness,
for we learned:

phrases.aramaic: עֵד אֶחָד עִבְרִי וְעֵד אֶחָד יְוָנִי – כָּשֵׁר!
phrases.english: one Hebrew witness and one Greek witness, it is valid!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלִיתַּכְשַׁר הַאי בְּעֵד אֶחָד עִבְרִי וְעֵד אֶחָד יְוָנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the same kind of question to the משנה's next case
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that both גיטין are invalid when the signatures alternate
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A mixed-language pair is valid, so each get should be validated by its own mixed pair

steps.title: זעירי again holds that both are valid
steps.stepSummary: As before, זעירי's teaching says both גיטין are valid in this case too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Indeed, זעירי teaches: both of them are valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same first answer as before: זעירי agrees with the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: זעירי's teaching does let each mixed pair validate its own גט. The argument is again only with the תנא of our משנה.

phrases.english: Indeed, זעירי teaches:
both of them are valid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא with the same approach as Step 7
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a תנא who agrees with the question's logic
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Everyone must hold that both גיטין are invalid
steps.terutzMaskana: זעירי validates both; our תנא disagrees

steps.title: Reversed signing could leave one get with a single witness
steps.stepSummary: Our תנא worries that one witness signed in reverse. Then three witnesses really signed one גט and only one signed the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And our תנא? Perhaps they signed in reverse, and three signed one גט and one signed the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why our משנה invalidates both גיטין in the mixed case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If one Greek signature was done in reverse, it may really belong to the other גט. Then one גט has three witnesses and the other has only one, and one witness is not enough for a גט. Since we cannot tell which גט is which, both are ruled invalid.
steps.whatToRemember: In both cases, זעירי validates each גט with its own witnesses. Our משנה is stricter because of גונדלית, the worry that signatures were written in reverse and belong to a different גט than they seem to.

phrases.english: And our תנא, why does he disagree?
perhaps they signed in reverse;
and three signed on one, and one on the other.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנָּא דִּידַן – דִּלְמָא גּוּנְדָּלִית חֲתֻים; וּתְלָתָא אַחַד, וְחַד אַחַד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the משנה's opposing view, matching Step 8
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a factual doubt about how the witnesses signed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Each mixed pair clearly belongs to its own get
steps.terutzMaskana: A reversed signature could leave one get with three witnesses and the other with one, so both are invalid

steps.title: A get continued in a second column, and witnesses signing in the wrong place
steps.stepSummary: If part of the גט spills into a second column and the witnesses sign below it, the גט is valid. If the witnesses sign at the top, on the side, or on the back of an ordinary גט, it is invalid.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the scribe left out part of the גט and wrote it in a second column, and the witnesses signed below, it is valid. If the witnesses signed at the top of the column, on the side, or on the back of an ordinary גט, it is invalid.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens. It first teaches where on the paper the witnesses must sign.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גט may run into a second column, as long as the witnesses sign at the bottom, after the text ends. Signatures at the top, on the side, or on the back do not close off the text, so an ordinary גט signed that way is invalid.

keyTerms.meaning: A column of writing on the sheet
An ordinary get, not the folded kind

steps.confusionAlert: Here דַּף means a column of writing, not a page of גמרא. Both columns are on the same sheet.

phrases.english: MISHNA:
If he left out part of the get
and wrote it in the second column,
and the witnesses are below, it is valid.
If witnesses signed at the top of the column,
on the side, or on its back,
in an ordinary get, it is invalid.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of the previous one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The witnesses must sign below the text. In an ordinary גט, signatures at the top, on the side, or on the back make it invalid.

steps.title: Two גיטין on one sheet with the witnesses in the middle
steps.stepSummary: The rule depends on how the two גיטין face each other. Top to top makes both invalid. End to end validates the one read in the same direction as the signatures. Top to end validates the one whose ending meets the signatures.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he placed the top of one גט next to the top of the other, with the witnesses in the middle, both are invalid. If he placed the end of one next to the end of the other, with the witnesses in the middle, the גט that is read together with the witnesses is valid. If he placed the top of one next to the end of the other, with the witnesses in the middle, the גט whose end leads into the witnesses is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now discusses two גיטין written on one sheet, with one set of signatures between them. It gives three possible arrangements.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Witnesses count only when they come after the end of a גט's text and read in the same direction. Top to top: neither גט ends at the signatures, so both are invalid. End to end: only the גט written in the same direction as the signatures is valid. Top to end: the גט whose last line leads into the signatures is valid.

keyTerms.meaning: Placed next to, lined up against
Are read together with it, meaning written in the same direction

steps.whyThisMatters: This case shows the basic rule behind all the signature cases: witnesses count only for the text that ends at their signatures and runs in the same direction.

phrases.english: If he placed the top of this one
next to the top of that one,
phrases.notes: Picture two גיטין on one sheet, written upside down to each other, with their opening lines facing each other.

phrases.english: and the witnesses are in the middle, both are invalid.

phrases.aramaic: סוֹפוֹ שֶׁל זֶה בְּצַד סוֹפוֹ שֶׁל זֶה,
phrases.english: The end of this one next to the end of that one,
and the witnesses are in the middle:
the one the witnesses are read with is valid.

phrases.aramaic: רֹאשׁוֹ שֶׁל זֶה בְּצַד סוֹפוֹ שֶׁל זֶה,
phrases.english: The top of this one next to the end of that one,
and the witnesses are in the middle:
the one whose end the witnesses are read at is valid.

steps.triggerLanguage: הִקִּיף רֹאשׁוֹ שֶׁל זֶה בְּצַד רֹאשׁוֹ שֶׁל זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the topic of where the signatures go. It now applies the idea to two גיטין on one sheet.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Signatures validate only the גט whose text ends at them and runs in the same direction as them.

steps.title: Mixed languages, and a scribe plus one witness
steps.stepSummary: A גט is valid if the text and the signatures are in different languages (Hebrew or Greek), or if one witness signs in Hebrew and the other in Greek. It is also valid if the scribe's handwriting and one witness's signature are confirmed.
steps.simpleTranslation: A גט written in Hebrew with its witnesses signed in Greek, or written in Greek with its witnesses signed in Hebrew, or with one witness in Hebrew and one in Greek, or with the writing of a scribe and one witness, is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה lists cases where the languages are mixed or where there is only one signing witness. It rules that all of them are valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The language of the signatures does not have to match the text, and the two witnesses do not have to match each other. The last case is different. When the scribe confirms his handwriting and one witness confirms his signature, that counts like two witnesses confirming the גט.

keyTerms.meaning: The scribe who wrote the get

steps.whyThisMatters: The ruling about one Hebrew witness and one Greek witness is the rule the גמרא relied on in steps 9 to 11.

phrases.english: A get written in Hebrew with its witnesses in Greek;
in Greek with its witnesses in Hebrew;

phrases.aramaic: עֵד אֶחָד עִבְרִי וְעֵד אֶחָד יְווֹנִי;
phrases.english: one witness in Hebrew and one witness in Greek;
the writing of a scribe and a witness: it is valid.
phrases.notes: The scribe recognizes his own handwriting and one witness confirms his signature. Together they count like two witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from where the witnesses sign to the language they sign in.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Mixed languages do not make a גט invalid. A scribe plus one witness is enough to confirm it.

steps.title: What a witness must write when he signs
steps.stepSummary: Each of these signatures is valid: 'So-and-so, witness.' 'Son of so-and-so, witness.' 'So-and-so son of so-and-so' without the word 'witness.' The careful people of ירושלים signed this last way.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he signed 'So-and-so, witness,' it is valid. 'Son of so-and-so, witness' is valid. 'So-and-so son of so-and-so' without writing 'witness' is valid, and this is what the careful-minded people of ירושלים used to do.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now explains how a witness may word his signature. It shows that the full formula is not required.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The witness may leave out his father's name, or his own name, or the word 'witness,' and the signature still works. The משנה adds that the most careful people in ירושלים skipped the word 'witness,' so leaving it out is not a lower standard.

phrases.english: "So-and-so, witness": it is valid.
"Son of so-and-so, witness": it is valid;
"So-and-so son of so-and-so,"
and he did not write "witness": it is valid,
and this is what the careful-minded people
of Jerusalem used to do.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the topic of signatures. It moves from language to the wording itself.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A signature is valid even without the father's name, without the witness's own name, or without the word 'witness'.

steps.title: Using nicknames for the husband and wife
steps.stepSummary: If the scribe wrote the husband's and wife's nicknames or surnames, the גט is valid.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he wrote his nickname and her nickname, it is valid.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה ends with one rule about how the husband and wife are named in the גט.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The topic changes from the witnesses' names to the couple's names. A well-known nickname or surname identifies them well enough, so the גט is valid.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה is lenient about form. Columns, mixed languages, short signatures, and nicknames are all valid. What matters is that the witnesses sign below the text and in the same direction as it.

phrases.english: If he wrote his nickname and her nickname, it is valid.
phrases.notes: "His" and "her" mean the husband and the wife named in the get.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the witnesses' names to the names of the husband and wife.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A גט that names the couple by nickname or surname is valid.

steps.title: Maybe it was really two separate גיטין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה's rule that a two-column גט is valid. Perhaps two different גיטין were written side by side, and someone cut away pieces so that the date of one and the witnesses of the other look like one גט.
steps.simpleTranslation: GEMARA: Let us worry that maybe these were really two גיטין. By chance, the date of the first one and the witnesses of the second one ended up next to each other. Then someone cut away the date of the second one and the witnesses of the first one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is questioning the משנה's ruling that a גט written in two columns, with witnesses signed under the second column, is valid. It suggests the 'two columns' might really be leftover pieces of two different גיטין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Picture two גיטין written side by side, with the second one placed higher on the page. Someone cuts off the top of the second (its date) and the bottom of the first (its witnesses). What is left looks like one גט in two columns: it opens with the first גט's date and ends with the second גט's witnesses. In that case the signatures do not belong to the text above them, so how can the משנה call it valid?

keyTerms.meaning: Let us be worried about; let us take into account
The first one / the later one

steps.confusionAlert: Nobody is saying the two-column גט is definitely a fake. The גמרא is only asking whether we need to worry that it might be one.

phrases.english: GEMARA:

phrases.aramaic: וְלֵיחוּשׁ דִּלְמָא הָנֵי תְּרֵי גִּיטֵּי הֲווֹ;
phrases.english: But let us worry that maybe these were two גיטין;
phrases.notes: This goes back to the משנה's case of a גט that runs into a second column.

phrases.english: and by chance the date of the first one
and the witnesses of the later one lined up next to each other;
and someone cut off the date of the later one
and the witnesses of the first one!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵיחוּשׁ דִּלְמָא הָנֵי תְּרֵי גִּיטֵּי הֲווֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling from step 12 that a גט spilling into a second column, with witnesses signed below it, is valid.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a two-column גט signed below the second column is valid.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The two columns could be pieces of two different גיטין that were cut to fit together, so the signatures would not belong to the text they seem to approve.

steps.title: Answer: there is empty space below the first column
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא, quoting רב, says the משנה is talking about a case where there is blank space below the first column, which shows nothing was cut off there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא said in the name of רב: The משנה is talking about a case where there is empty space below.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the worry by narrowing the משנה's case: there is blank paper under the first column.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the first גט's witnesses had been cut off from below, the column would end at the edge of the cut. Since there is clean blank space under the first column, no witnesses were cut away there. So the trick described in step 17 did not happen.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba said in the name of Rav:
It is when there is empty space below.
phrases.notes: He means blank space under the first column, showing nothing was cut off from there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא אָמַר רַב כְּשֶׁיֵּשׁ רֶיוַח מִלְּמַטָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the worry in step 17 by limiting the משנה to a case with blank space below the first column.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the משנה only refers to a specific physical layout.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The first column might have had witnesses below it that were cut away.
steps.terutzMaskana: The blank space below the first column shows that no witnesses were cut from it.

steps.title: Maybe only the date of the second גט was cut off
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא raises a new way to cheat: maybe the first גט was never signed, so it naturally has blank space below, and someone only cut off the date at the top of the second גט.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe someone cut off the date of the later one!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבי אבא's answer by suggesting a different trick that the blank space would not rule out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Blank space below only proves that no witnesses were cut from under the first column. But maybe the first גט was never signed at all, so the space below was empty from the start. Then a person only needed to cut away the date at the top of the second גט, and the two would still look like one גט in two columns.

phrases.english: But maybe the date of the later one
was cut off!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 18 by showing that blank space below does not rule out every way to cheat.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבא's answer that blank space below the first column removes the worry.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the first גט was never signed, its blank space below is natural, and cutting off only the date of the second גט could still create a fake two-column גט.

steps.title: Answer begins: bringing back רבי אבא's statement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to answer by repeating רבי אבא's statement in the name of רב about empty space below. The rest of the answer continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבי אבא said in the name of רב: The case is when there is empty space below;
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer to the new challenge by bringing back רבי אבא's words. The sentence is not finished here and continues right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא repeats the same statement on purpose, this time as the opening of a fuller answer to the new challenge. The words 'just as' show that more is being added to it. The full answer comes on the next amud.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not a needless repeat of step 18. The גמרא quotes רבי אבא again as the start of a new answer, and the sentence goes on after this point.

phrases.english: Just as Rabbi Abba said in the name of Rav:
It is when there is empty space below;

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְאָמַר רַבִּי אַבָּא אָמַר רַב כְּשֶׁיֵּשׁ רֶיוַח מִלְּמַטָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the challenge in step 19 by bringing back the statement from step 18 as the base for a fuller answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Extending an earlier limitation of the case (the answer continues past this point).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Blank space below alone does not rule out cutting off the date of the second גט.
steps.terutzMaskana: The answer builds on רבי אבא's 'space below' statement; its completion appears in the next lines.
